The retrieved evidence clusters into complementary facets: (1) long-run growth benefits from corporate tax cuts versus short-run boosts from personal cuts [d1]; (2) sector-specific gains (e.g., farming) [d2]; (3) mixed macro outcomes and wage effects [d4, d5, d6]; (4) distributional impacts of cuts for the rich [d3, d8]; (5) budgetary trade-offs from personal income tax cuts [d7]; and (6) short-run stimulus from targeted tax credits [d13]. These perspectives do not contradict each other; they address different beneficiaries, time frames, and policy designs.

The final answer synthesizes these complementary views without implying a single verdict on whether “tax cuts” are broadly beneficial, because the evidence shows benefits depend on tax type, timing, beneficiaries, and financing.

Tax cuts can benefit the economy in different ways depending on the type of tax and the time horizon considered. Corporate income tax cuts tend to generate large and persistent long-run gains by altering investment incentives, whereas personal income tax cuts mainly provide short-run stimulus and temporary GDP boosts [d1, d7]. Sector-specific cuts, such as those benefiting farmers under the TCJA, show targeted improvements in economic conditions for particular industries [d2]. However, not all tax cuts yield broad macroeconomic gains: cuts targeted at high earners are associated with higher inequality without significant effects on overall growth or unemployment [d3, d8], and corporate tax cuts are not linked to median wage growth across U.S. states [d6]. Empirical assessments of the TCJA also report higher investment and positive perceptions among small firms, alongside low unemployment, but these findings are limited to that policy episode and its projected effects [d4, d5]. Finally, temporary stimulus tax credits can provide immediate household relief and short-run support, as seen with the Recovery Act’s Making Work Pay credit [d13].

Sector-specific cuts, such as those benefiting farmers under the TCJA, show targeted improvements in economic conditions for particular industries [d2].
